Pattern_Foundry.inherited: From Color_Walls: The next sequence repeats forms across surfaces. Carry the distinction between the parts you begin with and the rule that determines their relationships.
Pattern_Foundry.question: How many places can one small decision change?
Pattern_Foundry.ontology: The source tile is a finite array of colour indices; the displayed field is a rule reading that array repeatedly. A motif and the rule repeating it are separable.
Pattern_Foundry.experiment: Take a coloured cube from the tile palette and release it over an off-centre grid cell. Watch the repeated preview. Make the same asymmetric motif on the mirror station and compare which copies reverse direction.
Pattern_Foundry.observe: One source-cell change appears in many preview positions. The simple-repeat station preserves orientation; MIRROR_XY reverses selected copies. An off-centre mark makes that difference visible.
Pattern_Foundry.limit: A large result is not necessarily many independent decisions. The repeated image cannot preserve a unique exception in just one copy because every copy reads the same source tile.
Pattern_Foundry.variation: Try to make a single off-centre mark appear only once in the repeated field. Its recurrence exposes the shared source. Independent exceptions would require a second layer or per-copy edits, a proposed extension.
Pattern_Foundry.handoff: The next station keeps the motif while changing the larger symmetry rule. Carry an asymmetric mark with you in memory; it will help you see which operation has been applied.
open_questions: Do not repeat older text claiming the 17 groups describe every pattern in the world. Here claims concern two finite rendered repeat rules, with museum hand reach still untested.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

Tutorial_Pattern.inherited: From Pattern_Foundry: The next station keeps the motif while changing the larger symmetry rule. Carry an asymmetric mark with you in memory; it will help you see which operation has been applied.
Tutorial_Pattern.question: What stays the same when you change the rule but keep the motif?
Tutorial_Pattern.ontology: A fundamental domain stores local decisions. A symmetry operation supplies a mapping between domain coordinates and copies; changing the mapping can reorganize the entire field without adding paint.
Tutorial_Pattern.experiment: Select a palette button and touch a few cells on the upright grid to create an asymmetric motif. Keep those cells fixed and cycle the group control. Then mirror or rotate the source using the station buttons.
Tutorial_Pattern.observe: Cycling the group changes the carpet while the source remains. Mirroring or rotating the source changes the input array itself. These are two distinct ways to obtain a new overall arrangement.
Tutorial_Pattern.limit: The palette and cell grid limit what can be drawn, and many different motifs can produce visually similar fields. A group name alone does not tell the complete story of the pattern, its maker, or its use.
Tutorial_Pattern.variation: Make a motif with an apparent symmetry, then add one cell that breaks it and watch which repetitions restore an overall symmetry anyway. A source-domain border is an available configuration axis but not a visitor button.
Tutorial_Pattern.handoff: The next room puts a repeated pattern onto a surface that extends through space. Watch for the difference between the rule of a field and the way that field is revealed to you.
open_questions: Touch painting depends on overlapping physics bodies. Config-after-ready limitations affect older grid loader; current museum applies config earlier. Do not promise all keyboard/controller aliases work here.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

Array_Patterns.inherited: From Tutorial_Pattern: The next room puts a repeated pattern onto a surface that extends through space. Watch for the difference between the rule of a field and the way that field is revealed to you.
Array_Patterns.question: When does repetition become an environment rather than a picture?
Array_Patterns.ontology: A pattern consists of a motif, a repetition rule and a surface receiving the result. A moving reveal can expose how a field is assembled in time.
Array_Patterns.experiment: At the tunnel console keep MOTIF and PALETTE fixed, adjust GROUP and watch the tube reskin. Use SPEED to separate how quickly it appears from the rule it displays. Compare the brick station by putting a coloured cube off-centre and following the staggered rows in its preview.
Array_Patterns.observe: The tunnel can change its rule without changing its source motif, and its reveal speed without changing its finished pattern. The brick preview offsets alternate rows, making boundaries fall in different places.
Array_Patterns.limit: A patterned surface can conceal the local rule that produced it. The tunnel is a finite rendered tube, and its historical palette names are presets, not evidence that a whole period had one style.
Array_Patterns.variation: Use a mismatched palette and motif intentionally, then describe the structural rule without relying on the style name. A room-wide comparison keeping all presets synchronized would be a future authoring tool.
Array_Patterns.handoff: The tube is finite, however continuous its pattern may look. The next room asks about an ideal pattern that repeats indefinitely in two independent directions. Keep the distinction between the rendered example you can inspect and the mathematical conditions under which a classification is made.
open_questions: Runtime access and controls require a museum walk; source-read only.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.

Symmetry_Seventeen.inherited: From Array_Patterns: The tube is finite, however continuous its pattern may look. The next room asks about an ideal pattern that repeats indefinitely in two independent directions. Keep the distinction between the rendered example you can inspect and the mathematical conditions under which a classification is made.
Symmetry_Seventeen.question: What assumptions make a catalogue of symmetries finite?
Symmetry_Seventeen.ontology: Wallpaper groups classify the symmetries of ideal patterns periodic in two independent directions on the Euclidean plane. Rotation, reflection, glide reflection and translation combine under that restriction.
Symmetry_Seventeen.experiment: Make an asymmetric motif with the tile editor’s grabbable colour cubes. Use the editor’s group navigation to compare how copies transform. Then inspect the cage’s marked rotational orders and distinguish its explanation from the editor’s live examples.
Symmetry_Seventeen.observe: Some choices reverse or rotate the motif as they repeat it. The cage marks 1,2,3,4,6 as compatible rotational orders and crosses 5 and 7; it is a static diagram, not a machine trying and failing to close a lattice.
Symmetry_Seventeen.limit: The count of seventeen applies under the periodic-plane assumptions; it does not contain every textile, finite ornament, quasicrystal, aperiodic tiling or cultural meaning of a pattern. The cage’s diagram illustrates a restriction; it does not prove the classification.
Symmetry_Seventeen.variation: Draw a fivefold-looking motif inside a repeatable cell and ask why a local motif can show a form the whole periodic lattice cannot adopt as a rotational symmetry. A nonperiodic tiling comparison would be a proposed additional artifact.
Symmetry_Seventeen.handoff: The next sequence studies change itself. Carry the habit of asking which quantities a rule relates and what must be held fixed before its answer can be interpreted.
open_questions: The editor defaults to legacy mirror mode; toggle symmetry mode before group-navigation claims. Do not repeat unsupported old claim that the Alhambra exhausted all seventeen groups.
Try the written encounter in the actual museum, alone and with a group. Check visibility, reach, the stated response and the handoff before accepting a room baseline.
